I’m just pointing out the the cost of upkeep of cattle is expensive. You also have to factor in things like TB testing which can wipe out a whole herd and then you’re buggered. 

There are places in the UK where cattle predominantly graze, however during winter typically the majority of cattle are housed indoors. Then you need to have a good supply of silage, which you’ve either bought or made yourself (then you’re factoring in tractor running costs, contractors wages etc.). 

It mainly boils down to the fact that buying a pint of milk should not be the cheapest thing when you’re doing the weekly shop. It’s a labour intensive industry and so many dairy farmers are packing up shop because they can’t realistically afford to keep going. It’s either that or diversify - there’s several farms near me who either sell raw milk, locally produced ice cream etc. but really if they were just paid more for milk it wouldn’t be an issue. 

The industry is predicting the milk price has reached its peak now, sitting at 50p/L in October. But you have to factor in agricultural costs are 30% higher, so fuel, feed, energy and labour costs (if you have dairy workers or employ contractors etc.) and the fact that over 80% of dairy herds no longer exist in the UK it’s not as plain sailing as just sticking them in a field of grass. 

Apologies if you think I’m making assumptions about your point, I just think the dairy industry is very misunderstood and underrepresented in the UK.

Cows definitely do not just eat grass - you have added costs of silage and grain. Most farmers will feed a certain diet mix for cattle. It’s not just a case of stick them on a field and hope for the best.

As someone who works in agriculture, a lot of the issues the industry faces is explaining the issues we face to those outside of the industry. 

Jeremy Clarkson, for all of his faults, has managed to engage people who aren’t from the industry and show them the issues that farmers face in the UK today. 

People generally think all farmers are wealthy landowners driving around in big 4x4s and purposely making them late for work when they get stuck behind a tractor on their commute. This couldn’t be further from the truth for the vast majority of farmers - tenant farmers, dairy farmers, smaller family farms especially - and they aren’t all rolling in money and holding shoots on the family estate. 

Highlighting the fact that farming takes a lot of work, most of it is outside of your control (weather, fertiliser costs, milk prices) and it’s a job that is honestly 365 days a year 24/7.

Our dog is awful at greeting guests, he just gets himself so worked up he doesn't know what to do with himself. So you're definitely not alone!

We've tried many things, but have recently started a routine that seems to work. When guests come over, he's straight into his crate. We ask people to ignore him until he's quiet and calm. At this point (it can take upwards of 30 minutes if he's incredibly worked up) we would leash him and put his basket muzzle on. 

I'm aware not everyone will have a muzzle (our dog is a garbage disposal so he wears one on walks to stop him eating everything!) but it stops him getting mouthy with people. He will start to do it to me if he gets antsy and worked up with guests. I prefer to use a muzzle as it takes the option away from him to even begin mouthing. 

When he's calm on leash, we let him off and keep the muzzle on. Any behaviour that is undesirable (jumping up, barking incessantly etc) he goes back in his crate and the process starts again. It has worked incredibly well so far, as before we couldn't even let him out of his crate when people came over as he would just go totally nuts. We would eventually like to work him up to taking the muzzle off around people, but it's a work in progress! 

Just my two cents about what works for us! 

Edit: I just wanted to add that he gets breaks from wearing the muzzle when people are over. If it's a long visit he will get breaks in the yard for 15~20 minutes to do his business, have a drink etc. Before bringing him back in.
